blocks.text: A multi-agent system is a team of autonomous agents that share one goal but act independently. Instead of one big model doing everything, specialized agents cooperate — and communication is what turns individuals into a team.

blocks.caption: Agent systems evolved from isolated programs into teams whose members talk to each other in natural language.

blocks.text: Without communication, agents duplicate work, contradict each other, and burn tokens re-discovering the same facts. With a shared protocol, they divide the work once and converge on a solution round after round.

blocks.sideText: When agents follow a shared protocol, coordination latency drops steadily as they learn each other's message patterns. Without one, latency stays high and unpredictable.

blocks.text: In a multi-agent system, agents exchange messages to share information, request actions, and coordinate toward a common goal.

blocks.caption: Agent A sends a message to Agent B, and Agent B processes it and can send a message to Agent C. This helps agents coordinate and work together.

blocks.alt: Sequence diagram: Agent A sends request(task) to Agent B, Agent B replies inform(result)

nodes.sublabel: Planner receives a task and analyzes it.
Result is returned to complete the task.

blocks.caption: This process ensures that each agent plays a specific role to achieve the goal efficiently.

nodes.label: Direct
nodes.sublabel: One-to-one. Fast and private, but every sender must know its receiver.

nodes.label: Broadcast
nodes.sublabel: One-to-all. Simple discovery, but floods the network as teams grow.

nodes.label: Pub-Sub
nodes.sublabel: Topic-based. Agents subscribe only to what they need.

nodes.label: Blackboard
nodes.sublabel: Shared memory. Agents read and write a common workspace.

blocks.sideText: Broadcast produces the most traffic because every agent receives every message. Direct messaging keeps volume low but requires each sender to know its receiver.

items: Addressed — a clear sender and receiver
Typed — inform, request, propose, or accept
Timestamped — so agents can order events

blocks.code:
class Message:
    def __init__(self, sender, receiver, content, msg_type, timestamp):
        self.sender = sender
        self.receiver = receiver
        self.content = content
        self.type = msg_type
        self.timestamp = timestamp
blocks.sideText: This code defines a message structure used by agents. It includes sender, receiver, content, type, and timestamp to ensure clear and meaningful communication.

blocks.text: A protocol defines who may talk, when, and in what format. Looking at the mix of message types tells you how much negotiating — versus plain reporting — your team actually does.

blocks.sideText: Most agent traffic is informational. Requests and proposals make up the negotiation layer, while accept messages close the loop on agreed actions.

blocks.alt: Multi-agent system architecture with message bus connecting agents
blocks.caption: A message bus connects every agent, so no agent needs a direct link to any other.

blocks.sideText: The planner breaks down the task and assigns work. The researcher finds the information and the executor carries out the action to get results.

blocks.caption: Each communication round feeds back into the agent's model of its teammates, improving the next round.

blocks.text: Tip: Agents should acknowledge every message they receive — silent failures are the hardest bugs to find in a multi-agent system.

items: Give every message a type and a timestamp
Prefer topic-based routing once the team grows past a handful of agents
Log every message; replaying a conversation beats guessing what happened
Communication is what turns individual agents into a team
Choose the messaging pattern that matches your team's size and shape
Structured, typed messages beat free-form text
Shared protocols cut coordination latency round after round

blocks.text: Check yourself before finishing this module:

questions.question: Why does broadcast messaging become a problem as a team grows?
options: It requires every agent to know its receiver in advance
Every agent receives every message, flooding the network
It cannot carry a message type or timestamp
It only works with a shared blackboard
questions.explanation: Broadcast is one-to-all, so traffic scales with team size. Topic-based Pub-Sub keeps volume down by letting agents subscribe only to what they need.

questions.question: Which four fields should every agent message carry?
options: Source IP, port, protocol, and size
questions.explanation: A well-formed message is addressed (sender/receiver), typed (inform/request/propose/accept), timestamped, and self-contained — the schema in this module lists sender, receiver, content, and type as the core fields.

questions.question: In the Planner → Researcher/Executor → Result example, what happens if the Researcher never reports back?
options: The Executor automatically takes over the research step
The Planner silently marks the task complete
The Result stays incomplete — the Planner is waiting on a message that never arrives
Nothing — Result only depends on the Executor
questions.explanation: The tree diagram shows Result depends on both Researcher and Executor. A silent failure from either agent stalls the whole task — which is exactly why every message should be acknowledged.
